lines.text: When a city camera stops working, who notices?
Audits found that in Philadelphia, only 32 percent of sampled police cameras were working properly.
In Pittsburgh, 45 of 163 cameras were not fully operational. Baltimore did not even track camera uptime.
And the AI on those cameras fails silently with them. Detectors can fall to 30 to 60 percent of their clean performance on corrupted images.
This is VisionDoctor: the AI that watches the cameras, so every other camera AI can be trusted.
It runs one loop. Scan, predict the damage, repair, verify, or call a human.
Step one: scan. Each camera first learns what healthy looks like, from its own clean footage.
Then eleven OpenCV 5 checks compare every new burst of frames against that reference.
Here the camera has been knocked five degrees. ORB features and a USAC MAGSAC homography measure the drift exactly.
Other checks catch haze, glare, smudges, occlusion, noise, colour casts, blur, exposure and frozen streams.
On real MOT17 street footage, VisionDoctor catches 91 percent of severe faults. A classic tamper detector catches 24.
Step two is our key idea. How much accuracy has the AI on this camera lost, with no labels at all?
In simulation, every degraded frame has an identical clean twin. How well the detector agrees with itself across the twins becomes the training target.
A gradient boosted model learns to predict that loss from the health signals alone.
Checked against real human labels, its predictions rank the true accuracy drop with a correlation of 0.5.
Step three: repair what software can fix. Realign, exposure, dehaze, white balance and denoise.
Every repair is bounded, and it only counts if a fresh scan and a fresh prediction confirm the recovery.
For drift, realignment restored 92 percent of the lost person detection accuracy, from 0.11 to 0.35 average precision. The clean camera scores 0.34.
If verification fails, the repair is rolled back, and the fault is escalated.
Step four: the agent. It reasons on Amazon Bedrock, but it never touches pixels or AWS directly.
It acts only through thirteen MCP tools, and a guard checks every single call.
In a live run, the model passed the wrong repair id. The guard blocked it. The agent re-planned, verified the fix, and only then closed the incident.
Physical faults, like a dirty lens, go to a person, ranked by predicted harm times camera importance, with faces blurred in the evidence.
Across forty simulated incidents, it chose the right outcome 75 percent of the time, and cut operator alerts by 65 percent.
Step five: the cloud. VisionDoctor is live on AWS Graviton4 in Mumbai, behind CloudFront and Cognito, with S3, DynamoDB and Bedrock.
One small Graviton instance scans twelve HD cameras 119 times a minute. That is about seven and a half dollars per million scans.
Here is the real console, running live on AWS right now.
Every camera shows its health and its predicted AI accuracy. Open one, and compare the reference with the live view.
Incidents wait for one-click approval, and every agent decision can be replayed, step by step.
Every number you have seen comes from our evaluation scripts on real labelled footage, with confidence intervals, and failure cases in the report.
What is new: label-free impact prediction, repairs that must prove themselves, technician-ready descriptions, and a queue ranked by real harm.
That helps security teams know which cameras really work, traffic teams trust their counts, factories catch drifting cameras, and technicians arrive with the right tool.
It is not perfect. Crowded scenes still cause false alarms, and we say so.
Scan, predict, repair, verify, escalate. Cameras you can trust, so the AI on them can be trusted too.
VisionDoctor. Built with OpenCV 5, on AWS.
